title: TCP Congestion Control
summary: How TCP infers and reacts to network congestion — slow start, additive growth, multiplicative backoff, and modern alternatives like BBR.

slides.markdown:
The internet's links and router buffers are **shared capacity**, not dedicated per connection. If every sender just blasted data as fast as its receiver's window allowed, routers would queue up, buffers would overflow, and packets would drop in a cascading collapse — everyone's throughput crashing at once.

**Congestion control** is TCP's self-imposed pacing: each sender maintains a **congestion window (cwnd)**, its own estimate of how much the *network* (not just the receiver) can currently absorb, and grows or shrinks it based on feedback.

A brand-new connection has no idea what the path can handle, so it starts conservatively — typically a few segments — and **doubles cwnd every round trip** as long as ACKs keep arriving cleanly.

![Congestion window doubling each round trip during slow start](assets/slow-start-growth.svg)

That's exponential growth, not gradual: it gets to useful throughput fast, but it also means slow start can overshoot and cause a loss event, which is exactly the signal it's watching for to know when to stop growing this aggressively.

assets.alt: Congestion window doubling each round trip during slow start

slides.markdown:
Once cwnd crosses the **slow-start threshold (ssthresh)** — typically set from the cwnd value at the last loss event — growth switches from exponential to **additive**: roughly one segment's worth of extra capacity per round trip instead of doubling.

This is deliberately cautious: near the estimated capacity of the path, TCP wants to probe for more bandwidth slowly rather than repeat the aggressive overshoot that slow start allows early on.

When loss is detected, classic TCP assumes it means congestion and reacts hard: **cut cwnd by half** (multiplicative decrease), then resume the cautious additive growth from there.

This asymmetry — grow slowly, back off fast — is deliberate. Overshooting capacity hurts everyone sharing the link, so the reaction to "you went too far" is much stronger than the reaction to "you can probably go a bit further."

Plot cwnd over time for a classic (loss-based) TCP connection and you get a **sawtooth**: additive growth climbing steadily, then a sharp halving at each loss event, repeating indefinitely.

![Sawtooth congestion window graph over time with growth and halving](assets/congestion-sawtooth.svg)

That sawtooth isn't a flaw to fix — it's TCP continuously probing for more available bandwidth and backing off when it finds the ceiling, which is why a single well-behaved TCP connection rarely uses 100% of a link's true capacity at every instant.

assets.alt: Sawtooth congestion window graph over time with growth and halving

slides.markdown:
Three duplicate ACKs trigger **fast retransmit** (resend the missing segment without waiting for a timeout) paired with **fast recovery**: instead of dropping all the way back to slow start, cwnd is halved and growth resumes from there additively.

This matters because a full timeout-triggered restart from slow start is much more disruptive to throughput than a single halving — fast recovery treats an isolated loss (likely transient congestion) more gently than a full timeout (likely a more serious problem).

| | Reno/Tahoe (classic) | CUBIC (modern default) |
|---|---|---|
| Growth after loss | Linear, restarts from ssthresh | Cubic function, fast near ssthresh then flattens |
| Behavior on high-BDP links | Recovers slowly, underutilizes | Recovers bandwidth faster |
| Where used | Legacy/simple systems | Default on Linux since 2.6.19 |

CUBIC exists because linear growth was too slow to refill a long-fat pipe (high bandwidth-delay product) after a single loss — it's the same grow/back-off idea, tuned for modern high-capacity links.

Loss-based algorithms (Reno, CUBIC) treat packet loss as the congestion signal — but on links with large buffers, loss can lag far behind actual congestion, causing **bufferbloat**.

**BBR** takes a different approach: it actively measures the path's bandwidth and round-trip time, builds a model of the pipe, and paces sending to match that model directly — reacting to *measured conditions* rather than waiting for a drop.

Routers with large buffers seem helpful — more room means fewer drops. But loss-based congestion control needs loss to know when to slow down. Oversized buffers just let queues grow and grow, adding latency to every packet in line, before a drop finally happens.

The result: a bulk download can add hundreds of milliseconds of latency to an unrelated video call sharing the same router, with no packet loss to blame. See [Packet Capture — tcpdump & Wireshark](packet-capture-tcpdump-wireshark) for spotting queuing delay in practice.

| | Loss-based (Reno/CUBIC) | Model-based (BBR) |
|---|---|---|
| Congestion signal | Packet loss | Measured bandwidth + RTT |
| Behavior with big buffers | Can queue up badly before reacting (bufferbloat) | Avoids filling buffers unnecessarily |
| Maturity/deployment | Decades of production tuning | Newer, used by YouTube/Google infra, growing elsewhere |

Decide by symptom: chronic latency spikes without loss point toward a loss-based algorithm queuing behind bufferbloat — a candidate for a model-based approach instead.

slides.sectionTitle: Pitfall: congestion window is not receive window
slides.markdown:
**Wrong belief:** "If throughput is low, the receiver must be slow — check the app on the other end."

**Why it's wrong:** low throughput can just as easily come from the **congestion window** being small because the *network path* is lossy or congested — nothing to do with how fast the receiver's app is reading.

**Correct model:** TCP throughput is capped by `min(rwnd, cwnd)`. Diagnosing a slow connection means checking both independently — a healthy receiver with a struggling network path will still look slow.
